<previous>e. The ability to try new application protocols at the grassroots, and see whether they become popular, was very important in the evolution of the Internet up through the introduction of the web.

However, the Internet has been progressively moving away from the endto-end principle. I already alluded to one example: firewalls that filter at the application layer. I will mention firewalls again in Section 9.6.2. However, there have also been other non-security-related forces leading away from the</previous>
<target>##### 402

end-to-end principle; I will examine one in Section 9.4.3. One upshot of this is that today it may no longer be possible to just start using a new application protocol with its associated port number. Traffic on the new port number might well be blocked as it traverses the Internet.

This helps explain a popular use of web services, which I mention in Chapter 10. This form of communications middleware is often configured to package application programs’ messages into web traffic, in effect layering yet another protocol on top of the web’s application-layer protocol. This approach helps circumvent obstacles to new application-layer protocols within the Internet. For this chapter, I will stick with the traditional layers, topping out at the application layer.</target>
